milestones.title: Work begins on Nagoya Castle
milestones.detail: Tokugawa Ieyasu orders some twenty daimyo to build a new castle on the Atsuta plateau as the capital of Owari Province, replacing flood-prone Kiyosu. The stone base of the main keep is finished by August.

milestones.title: Keep completed; Kiyosu moves to Nagoya
milestones.detail: The main keep is completed in December 1612 and a grid of streets is laid out south of the castle. Between 1612 and 1616 almost all of Kiyosu's roughly 2,700 townhouses, with 110 temples and three shrines, are moved to the new town.

milestones.title: Manji fire and the widening of Hirokōji
milestones.detail: A great fire burns nearly 3,000 houses. Afterwards the broad street of Hirokōji is opened at the southern edge of the grid.

milestones.title: Tokugawa Muneharu promotes Nagoya as a commercial city
milestones.detail: The seventh lord of Owari takes office and encourages trade and entertainment in the castle town until he is confined by the shogunate in 1739.

milestones.title: Nagoya becomes a prefectural capital
milestones.detail: With the abolition of the feudal domains, Nagoya Domain becomes Nagoya Prefecture, renamed Aichi the following year. The prefectural office is placed inside the castle.

milestones.title: Railway station opens
milestones.detail: The government railway, now the Tōkaidō Main Line, opens its station at Nagoya on 1 May 1886.

milestones.title: City of Nagoya incorporated
milestones.detail: Nagoya becomes a city on 1 October 1889, covering 13.44 square kilometres around today's Naka and Higashi wards with about 157,000 people.

milestones.title: Nōbi earthquake
milestones.detail: The Mino-Owari earthquake of 28 October 1891 causes heavy damage in the city and to Nagoya Castle.

milestones.title: Electric trams begin running
milestones.detail: Street tramway service starts on 6 May 1898. The network lasts until 1974.

milestones.title: Merger quadruples the city's area
milestones.detail: Surrounding towns and villages are merged into Nagoya in 1921. The city grows from 38.9 square kilometres at the 1920 census to 149.95 at the 1925 census, when it becomes Japan's third-largest city.
milestones.source: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/名古屋市 ; https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/都道府県庁所在地と政令指定都市の人口順位

milestones.title: Population passes one million
milestones.detail: The census of 1 October 1935 counts 1,082,816 residents, the first above one million. Aircraft and machinery works make Nagoya a leading industrial city.

milestones.title: Air raids burn the city and the castle
milestones.detail: Firebombing from March 1945 burns almost a quarter of the city, and Nagoya Castle's keep is destroyed on 14 May. The population falls from 1.33 million in 1940 to under 600,000.

milestones.title: Subway opens
milestones.detail: The first section of the Nagoya Municipal Subway, now the Higashiyama Line, opens between Nagoya Station and Sakaemachi on 15 November 1957.

milestones.title: Ise Bay Typhoon; castle keep rebuilt
milestones.detail: Typhoon Vera strikes on 26 September 1959 and its storm surge floods the southern part of the city. In the same year the castle keep is rebuilt in concrete.

milestones.title: Tōkaidō Shinkansen reaches Nagoya
milestones.detail: The high-speed line between Tokyo and Osaka opens on 1 October 1964 with a station at Nagoya.

milestones.title: Expo 2005
milestones.detail: The World Expo is held from 25 March to 25 September 2005 in Nagakute and Seto, just east of the city.

notes: Start date: 1610 is when construction of Nagoya Castle and its planned town began; the city counts its founding from that year, and the town was populated by moving Kiyosu wholesale in 1612-16. Two older things stood on the ground of today's city and are not treated as its founding: an earlier small castle at Nagoya (built by the Imagawa in 1521-28, held by the Oda, abandoned about 1582), and Atsuta Shrine, a separate shrine and Tōkaidō post town to the south whose traditional founding around AD 100 is legend. Population before 1873 is thin: the only figures found are Chandler's estimates at 50-year steps (65,000 to 93,000), which may leave out the samurai households; the first government count in 1873 is a third higher than his 1850 figure, so the Edo-period points are probably low. No figure was found for 1610-1649. The 1873 and 1879 figures use differently drawn urban areas. From 1889 the figures are for the city as bounded at each date; the jump between 1920 and 1925 is the 1921 merger. Register-based counts before 1920 overstate the population, so police-survey counts were used for 1908 and 1913. The UN series from 1950 covers the whole Chūkyō urban agglomeration, several times the municipal figure, so expect a step at 1950. Landmarks: pre-modern coverage is limited to the castle keep, the only old structure with a sourced height. The height given for the 1959 concrete keep is that of the original it reproduces, marked estimated. Left out for lack of a sourced height: Atsuta Shrine, Ōsu Kannon (moved to Nagoya in 1612), Nagoya City Hall (1933), the Aichi Prefectural Office and the Nagoya Dome.
